How Much Is $23 an Hour a Year? Full Pay & Budget Breakdown

Quick Answer

$23 an hour is $47,840 a year gross on a standard full-time schedule. That's $920 a week and $3,986.67 a month before taxes.

Got a job offer at $23.00 an hour? The first questions are obvious: what does that add up to over a year, what actually lands in your bank account, and can you live on it? At $23 an hour you're earning more than three times the federal minimum wage, and your gross pay hits $47,840 a year, close to $50,000. But the headline number isn't the whole story. What you take home, and what it covers, is what matters.

Building pay tools here, the mix-up we see most is gross pay versus take-home pay. Schedules, unpaid holidays, payroll taxes, and local rent can make the same $23 rate feel very different from one person to the next. A full-time worker with paid time off lives a different financial life than a contractor taking unpaid weeks between jobs.

This guide runs the numbers for $23 an hour across every pay period, shows what unpaid leave and overtime do to your year, breaks down 2026 federal and state taxes, and builds a realistic monthly budget for a $47,840 income.

Calculate $23 an Hour Pay

$23 an Hour at a Glance: The Quick Answer

On a standard full-time schedule, 40 hours per week for all 52 weeks of the year (2,080 working hours), $23 an hour equals $47,840.00 per year gross, before taxes and benefit deductions.

Here's what that $47,840 looks like at the usual pay frequencies, before anything is withheld:

Where Does $23 an Hour Put You in the US Workforce?

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the U.S. Census Bureau put the national median wage for full-time workers somewhere between $48,000 and $50,000 a year. At $47,840 per year, $23 an hour puts you right in the middle of the American workforce.

What $23 an hour buys depends a lot on where you live:

  • Low-to-Mid Cost of Living Areas (e.g., Indiana, Ohio, Missouri, Oklahoma): $47,840 a year goes a long way here. One person can rent an apartment, keep a car on the road, cover groceries, and still put money into emergency savings.
  • High Cost of Living Metros (e.g., Los Angeles, Seattle, Boston, New York City): Housing eats into a $47,840 salary fast. In these cities, splitting rent with a roommate or partner is often the only way to keep housing under 40% of your income.

The Exact Math: How $23 an Hour Converts Across Every Pay Period

Payroll works off a standard baseline: a 40-hour week across 52 weeks gives you 2,080 scheduled hours a year.

Annual Gross = Hourly Wage × Weekly Hours × Paid Weeks

Calculation: $23.00 × 40 hours × 52 weeks = $47,840.00 gross annual income

Pay Period Calculation Formula Gross Amount Payroll Frequency Notes
Hourly Rate Base contracted wage $23.00 Straight-time rate per hour
Daily (8 Hours) $23.00 × 8 hours $184.00 Standard full-time day
Weekly $23.00 × 40 hours $920.00 52 pay periods per year
Biweekly $23.00 × 80 hours (or $47,840 ÷ 26) $1,840.00 Paid every two weeks (26 checks/year)
Semi-Monthly $47,840.00 ÷ 24 $1,993.33 Paid twice per month (24 checks/year)
Monthly Average $47,840.00 ÷ 12 $3,986.67 Derived from annual (not weekly × 4)
Quarterly $47,840.00 ÷ 4 $11,960.00 4 quarters per calendar year
Annual Total $23.00 × 2,080 hours $47,840.00 Full-time working year

How Unpaid Time Off Changes Your Annual Earnings

The $47,840 figure assumes 52 fully paid weeks. If your job includes paid time off (PTO), paid vacation, and paid federal holidays, you get paid for all 52 weeks no matter which days you take off. Your gross pay stays at $47,840.

But if your employer doesn't offer paid leave, or you take unpaid time off for travel, personal reasons, or a shutdown, every unpaid week cuts your annual pay by 40 hours of wages ($920.00 gross):

52 Paid Weeks (Includes PTO)

40 hours/week · 0 unpaid weeks

$47,840.00 gross / year

Standard baseline compensation

50 Paid Weeks (2 Unpaid Weeks Off)

40 hours/week · 2 weeks unpaid leave

$46,000.00 gross / year

-$1,840.00 reduction in annual earnings

Just two unpaid weeks drops your paid hours to 2,000 a year and your gross pay to $46,000.00. Four weeks of unpaid leave takes it down to $44,160.00. So when a job offer has no PTO, factor that into the yearly number before you compare it to anything else.

Overtime Math: Pushing $23/Hour Past $56,000 to $65,000

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), non-exempt employees who work more than 40 hours in a week must get overtime pay of at least 1.5 times their regular rate (time-and-a-half).

Overtime Hourly Rate = Base Wage × 1.5 = $23.00 × 1.5 = $34.50 / hour

Every hour worked past 40 adds $34.50 straight to your gross paycheck.

At $34.50 an hour, regular overtime adds up fast:

Weekly Schedule Regular Weekly Pay Overtime Weekly Pay Total Weekly Gross Annual Gross (52 Weeks)
40 Hours (0 OT) $920.00 $0.00 $920.00 $47,840.00
45 Hours (5 hrs OT) $920.00 +$172.50 $1,092.50 $56,810.00
48 Hours (8 hrs OT) $920.00 +$276.00 $1,196.00 $62,192.00
50 Hours (10 hrs OT) $920.00 +$345.00 $1,265.00 $65,780.00

Five hours of overtime a week adds $172.50 a week. That's an extra $8,970.00 a year, lifting your gross pay to $56,810.00. Ten hours a week adds $17,940.00 a year, pushing your gross pay to $65,780.00. How Much Is $23 an Hour After 2026 Taxes? (Take-Home Breakdown)

Gross pay is what you earn on paper. Take-home pay is what hits your bank account. To work out realistic take-home pay on $47,840, we use the 2026 federal tax brackets, FICA payroll taxes, and typical state tax rates for a single filer taking the standard deduction.

1. Mandatory 2026 Federal Tax & FICA Breakdown

  • Gross Annual Salary: $47,840.00
  • 2026 Standard Deduction (Single Filer): $16,100.00
  • Taxable Income: $47,840.00 − $16,100.00 = $31,740.00
  • 2026 Federal Income Tax Calculation:
    • 10% on the first $12,400.00 = $1,240.00
    • 12% on the remaining $19,340.00 ($31,740 − $12,400) = $2,320.80
    • Total Federal Income Tax: $1,240.00 + $2,320.80 = $3,560.80 (Effective federal tax rate: ~7.44%)
  • Mandatory FICA Payroll Taxes (7.65% on full gross):
    • Social Security (6.2%): $47,840.00 × 6.2% = $2,966.08
    • Medicare (1.45%): $47,840.00 × 1.45% = $693.68
    • Total FICA Withholdings: $3,659.76
  • Total Mandatory Federal Withholdings (Income Tax + FICA): $3,560.80 + $3,659.76 = $7,220.56

2. State Tax Variations & Net Take-Home Pay

State income tax is what makes the same paycheck look different from one state to another. Here's how annual and monthly take-home pay shakes out in three typical state tax situations:

State Tax Tier Representative States Annual Net Pay Monthly Net Biweekly Net Check
No State Income Tax (0%) Texas, Florida, Washington, Tennessee, Nevada, Wyoming, Alaska, South Dakota ~$40,619.44 ~$3,385.00 ~$1,562.00
Moderate State Tax (~4.5%) Illinois, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Arizona, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio ~$38,466.00 ~$3,205.00 ~$1,479.00
Higher State Tax (~6%) California, New York, New Jersey, Oregon, Minnesota, Massachusetts ~$37,749.00 ~$3,146.00 ~$1,452.00

These figures use the 2026 federal brackets, standard deduction, and FICA for a single taxpayer with no dependents. Voluntary deductions like health insurance or 401(k) contributions will lower both your taxable income and your take-home pay. For a line-by-line look at your deductions, read our guide on how to calculate taxes on a paycheck.

A Realistic 50/30/20 Monthly Budget on $23 an Hour

With take-home pay between $3,205.00 and $3,385.00 a month, a clear budget keeps you from running short at the end of the month. The 50/30/20 budget framework is a simple way to cover living costs and still save something.

50% Needs
~$1,600 – $1,690 / mo

• Rent/Housing: ~$1,000 – $1,100 (Max recommended rent based on the 30% gross rule)
• Utilities & Internet: ~$190 – $210
• Groceries & Household Goods: ~$300 – $320
• Transportation & Insurance: ~$200 – $220

30% Wants
~$960 – $1,015 / mo

• Dining Out & Socializing: ~$250 – $280
• Entertainment & Subscriptions: ~$80 – $100
• Clothing & Personal Care: ~$100 – $120
• Hobbies, Fitness & Travel Buffer: ~$530 – $550

20% Savings & Debt
~$640 – $677 / mo

• Emergency Fund: ~$250 – $300 (Build 3–6 months of essential living expenses)
• Roth IRA / 401(k): ~$250 – $300 ($3,000–$3,600/year invested)
• Extra Debt Reduction: ~$100 – $140

The Housing Rule at $23/Hour: Living Solo vs. Having a Roommate: A common rule of thumb is keeping housing under 30% of your gross monthly pay. On $3,986.67 a month gross, that puts your target rent around $1,000.00 to $1,100.00 per month ($47,840 × 0.30 ÷ 12 ≈ $1,196 max ceiling). Where one-bedroom apartments run $1,400 to $1,800, sharing a place with a roommate drops your share to $750–$900, which frees up hundreds of dollars a month for savings and emergencies.

Common Budgeting & Paycheck Math Mistakes on $23/Hour

These are the mistakes that trip people up most when they're planning around $23 an hour:

Mistake 1: Multiplying weekly pay by 4 to project monthly income ($3,680 vs. $3,986.67).

A $920 weekly check times 4 gives $3,680.00. But a year has 52 weeks, not 48, so an average month has 4.333 weeks (52 ÷ 12). Your real average monthly gross is $3,986.67. Budgeting on 4 weeks undercounts your year by four full weeks of pay ($3,680 a year).

Mistake 2: Confusing biweekly (26 checks) with semi-monthly (24 checks) schedules.

Biweekly pay means 26 paychecks a year at $1,840.00 gross each. Semi-monthly means 24 checks at $1,993.33 each. The annual gross is the same ($47,840), but each biweekly check is smaller, because two months a year have three paychecks instead of two.

Mistake 3: Forgetting mandatory FICA taxes (7.65%).

Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) come out of every dollar you earn, starting with the first one. On a $47,840 salary, FICA totals $3,659.76 a year ($140.76 biweekly). Forget FICA and your take-home estimate will be way off.

Mistake 4: Budgeting rent and fixed debt against gross earnings.

Never sign a lease based on the $3,986 gross monthly figure. Budget against what actually lands in your account ($3,146 to $3,385/month, depending on state taxes and benefit deductions).

Mistake 5: Assuming overtime is permanent base income.

Employers can cut back or freeze overtime when work slows down. Keep your fixed costs (rent, car, utilities) inside your regular 40-hour take-home pay, and put overtime money toward debt or savings.

Limitations

  1. Federal-only take-home: the after-tax figures in this guide use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. State and local income taxes are excluded and would lower the check further.
  2. The 2,080-hour assumption: the $47,840 headline needs 40 paid hours in every week of the year. Fewer scheduled hours, or weeks of unpaid leave, scale it down proportionally.
  3. Overtime is conditional: the overtime scenarios require non-exempt status, an employer who schedules the hours, and hours actually worked past 40 in a single week.
  4. Benefits sit outside the math: health premiums, 401(k) contributions, and other payroll deductions are not subtracted unless a section says so — your deposit will be smaller than the tax-only estimate.
  5. Withholding vs. liability: each paycheck's withholding follows payroll tables and can differ from the annual figures sketched here; any difference settles when you file your return.
  6. Not tax advice: these are planning estimates for one filing profile. Credits, a second job, or a different filing status change your real numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions About $23 an Hour

How much is $23 an hour a year?

Work full-time, 40 hours a week for 52 paid weeks (2,080 hours), and $23 an hour comes to $47,840 a year gross, before taxes and deductions. Take 2 weeks of unpaid vacation (50 paid weeks) and it drops to $46,000.

How much is $23 an hour per month?

At 40 hours a week, $23 an hour averages $3,986.67 a month before taxes ($47,840 divided by 12). A common slip is multiplying your $920 weekly pay by 4 to get $3,680. That undercounts your year by $3,680, because calendar months average 4.33 weeks, not 4.

How much is $23 an hour on a biweekly paycheck?

On a biweekly schedule (every two weeks, 26 paychecks a year), $23 an hour pays $1,840.00 gross for 80 hours ($23 × 80). After 2026 federal income tax and FICA (7.65%), a single filer taking the standard deduction in a state with no income tax takes home about $1,562 per paycheck.

How much is $23 an hour after taxes?

For a single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction ($16,100), federal income tax is $3,560.80 and FICA (Social Security and Medicare) is $3,659.76. In states with no income tax, like Texas or Florida, take-home pay is about $40,619.44 a year (~$3,385/month). In states with moderate income tax (~4.5%), it's about $38,466 (~$3,205/month). In higher-tax states (~6%), it's roughly $37,749 (~$3,146/month).

What is the overtime rate for $23 an hour?

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), time-and-a-half is 1.5 times your regular rate. At $23 an hour, your overtime rate is $34.50 ($23 × 1.5). Five hours of overtime a week adds $172.50 in weekly gross pay ($8,970 over 52 weeks), lifting your total gross pay to $56,810.00 a year.

How much is $23 an hour working part-time?

It depends on your hours, at the same $23 rate. At 20 hours a week you earn $460 a week, or $23,920 a year (52 weeks). At 25 hours, it's $575 a week or $29,900 a year. At 30 hours, $690 a week or $35,880 a year. At 35 hours, $805 a week or $41,860 a year. Those are gross figures before taxes. Part-time roles can also come with fewer benefits than full-time ones, so compare the whole offer, not just the hourly rate.

Key Takeaways & Next Steps

Core Summary for $23/Hour Earners

  • Standard Annual Baseline: Full-time at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year, comes to $47,840.00 gross per year (2,080 working hours).
  • Monthly Average: Monthly gross is $3,986.67. Remember, a calendar month averages 4.33 weeks, not 4.
  • 2026 Net Take-Home Pay: After federal income tax ($3,560.80) and FICA ($3,659.76), take-home pay runs from ~$37,749 to ~$40,619 annually (~$3,146 to ~$3,385/month), depending on state taxes.
  • Overtime Potential: Overtime pays $34.50/hour. Five hours a week adds an extra $8,970/year, lifting gross pay to $56,810.
  • Housing Target: Keep housing around $1,000 to $1,100/month so there's still room to save.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Full-time gross pay is $47,840 a year, or $3,986.67 a month before taxes.
  2. Overtime can lift the same rate to $56,810 a year.
  3. Don't multiply weekly pay by 4 for a monthly figure. That undercounts the year, because calendar months average more than 4 weeks.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
